Beneath this transparent roof grows a garden.

Thousands of tiny, copper-colored organisms line the dome’s inner surface, harvesting the dim sunlight. They provide the wanderer with sugars; in return, it supplies them with warmth, water, and minerals. Well-fed individuals glow amber around the edges. A starving one becomes almost perfectly clear.

The wanderer has no recognizable face. At the front of its body hangs a cluster of twelve soft feelers, surrounding a narrow mouth. It sweeps these feelers across the ground to taste mineral deposits and detect the electrical activity of buried life. When it finds a colony of ribbonworms, it presses its mouth to the soil and releases a warm digestive foam. A few minutes later, it drinks the resulting broth.

Its eyes are scattered along its flanks: small black beads tucked beneath overlapping folds of skin. They see little detail, but together they give it an almost uninterrupted view of the horizon.

An adult is roughly the size of a horse, but its body hangs low between six long, jointed legs. Each foot opens into a fan of flexible toes that spreads its weight over the marsh crust. When the crust begins to break, the toes curl upward and the creature slides forward on its belly, paddling until it reaches firmer ground.

Its skin is charcoal-gray and finely ridged, like cooled lava. Along its spine rises a row of translucent chambers, each shaped like a pear standing on its narrow end. By day—or what passes for day in the unmoving twilight—they resemble cloudy glass. When the lanternback feeds, they fill with a slow amber glow.

The light comes from colonies of microbes living inside the chambers. The lanternback supplies them with minerals filtered from the mud; in return, they produce nutrients it cannot make for itself. A healthy animal carries an even glow. During lean seasons, individual chambers go dark.

The lanternback has no face in the familiar sense. Beneath the front of its body hangs a ring of soft, fingerlike feelers surrounding a narrow mouth. It drags these through shallow pools, tasting for mats of iron-rich organisms. Two dark pits above the feeding ring detect heat, while a broad membrane under its throat reads vibrations in the ground. It can sense another lanternback walking several hundred meters away.

Its most striking behavior occurs when storms approach.

Before the first gust reaches the marsh, lanternbacks gather into small circles, their heads turned inward. They hook their outer legs together and lower themselves until their bellies touch the ground. The arrangement prevents individuals from being rolled away by the wind. Young shelter beneath the adults, pressed into the warm spaces between their bodies.

Within these huddles, their back chambers pulse. Light-sensitive patches along their flanks allow neighboring animals to see the signals even through thick fog. A quick flash means *shift your weight*. A slow ripple brings the circle tighter.

Their eggs look like flat stones. Adults bury them at the warm edges of mineral springs, then return repeatedly to turn them with their mouth-feelers. Newly hatched lanternbacks are pale and completely dark. They acquire their glowing microbes by licking the chambers of an adult.

An old lanternback can be recognized by its scratched, uneven lanterns and its shortened stride. On still evenings, it may stand alone in a pool with its lights reflected beneath it, gently stirring the mud for food while the fixed sun burns low on the horizon.
